passage:
My cousin Simran waited by the phone every Sunday last autumn after she moved to Pune. At first Rekha wrote back the same day with long voice notes. By October the replies were a line or two, sometimes two weeks late. I saw Simran read them twice and put the phone face down. She didn't say much; I think it stung. Then she made a card for Rekha and marked the December holidays on the calendar to visit. At dinner she said, "We'll meet in December. She still likes me. We just live different days now." I couldn't tell if she believed it.

- Manav

qa.q: When did Simran plan to see Rekha?
What might Simran have felt when she read Rekha's short replies twice and put the phone face down?
qa.a: Hurt, though Manav can only guess that it stung.

qa.q: What could Simran do to stay close to Rekha?
qa.a: Keep in touch on holidays, like the card and the December visit, while accepting that they may drift and still stay fond.

qa.q: How might Rekha see the situation?
qa.a: She may be busy with days of her own and may still care, though the passage does not say why her replies got shorter.

grounding: An old friend replies less after the move and it hurts, but the child keeps in touch on holidays and accepts drifting, seen by her cousin.
